summary: Defines the part of the management database used to manage network interfaces, such as the port a device uses to connect to a network. It updates and replaces RFC 1573, and was in turn replaced by RFC 2863.

eli5.summary: Every computer has plugs to connect to networks. This defines how a manager checks on each plug: whether it is on, busy, or having trouble.

questions: what is the interfaces group mib
how to monitor network interfaces with snmp
why does snmp use 64 bit counters
subtitle: How SNMP describes network interfaces: one table row per sub-layer, 64-bit counters, and clearer up and down states.

tldr.problem: The interfaces group of MIB-II treated each interface as one simple, static row. Real devices stack sub-layers, add and remove interfaces at run time, and run fast enough to wrap 32-bit counters in minutes.
tldr.mechanism: The IF-MIB gives each sub-layer its own ifTable row and links them with an ifStackTable. It adds 64-bit counters, ifHighSpeed, ifName, ifAlias, ifCounterDiscontinuityTime, new ifOperStatus states and a trap-enable control.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that replaced RFC 1573 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 2863.

today: RFC 2233 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 2863, so current work should follow that document. It replaced RFC 1573.

sections.title: Why the Interfaces Group Changed
sections.content:
This memo defines the part of the MIB used to manage network interfaces. It revisits the interfaces group of MIB-II in light of the many media-specific MIB modules written since. The RFC says experience showed the MIB-II model to be too simplistic or static for some media, so it standardizes the evolution of the model and fills the resulting gaps. It also folds in the extensions from RFC 1229.

The module re-specifies the MIB-II group in SNMPv2 SMI form with identical semantics, and adds new definitions. The key words MUST and MUST NOT are used as in RFC 2119.
sections.eli5: The old way of listing a device's network plugs was too simple for modern gear. This note upgrades it without breaking what already worked.

sections.title: Sub-Layers and the Interface Stack
sections.content:
An interface is often several layers, for example PPP over an HDLC link over an RS232-like connector. Rejected designs used one row per whole interface with pointers between modules. The adopted design gives each sub-layer its own conceptual row in the ifTable and adds the ifStackTable, which uses integer pointers to say which row sits above or below which. This supports both upward multiplexing (such as MLP sharing several serial lines) and downward multiplexing.

Packet counters are defined as counting what is delivered to a higher layer. That includes a bridge's forwarding module, a higher sub-layer in the stack, or the local IP module at the top. The RFC advises keeping the number of ifTable entries to the minimum needed, and it strongly recommends that connection-oriented sub-layers do not get a row per virtual circuit.
sections.eli5: A network plug is like a sandwich with layers. Each layer gets its own line on the list, and a second list says which layer sits on top of which.

sections.title: Tables, Numbering and Names
sections.content:
The module has four tables: ifTable (from MIB-II), ifXTable (added and replacement objects), ifStackTable and ifRcvAddressTable (media-level addresses the interface receives, whose exact meaning media-specific MIBs must define).

For numbering, the rule that ifIndex must be less than ifNumber is dropped so interfaces can be added and removed dynamically, which allows holes in the table. A removed interface's index is not reused by a different interface until the next re-initialization. New values are recommended to stay small integers starting at 1. ifCounterDiscontinuityTime records the last counter discontinuity, and managers must discard a computed difference if it changed between polls.

For names, ifName holds the device's local name for the interface (for example wan1), while ifAlias is a non-volatile name a manager can set, kept across reboots. The ifSpecific object is deprecated, and ifType now uses the IANAifType textual convention so IANA can add values without reissuing this document.
sections.eli5: Each plug gets a number and a name. The number can have gaps, and a manager can also give a plug a nickname that survives a reboot.

sections.title: Counters and Speed
sections.content:
A 32-bit octet counter wraps fast on quick links. The RFC gives 57 minutes at 10Mbs, 5.7 minutes at 100Mbs and 34 seconds at 1Gbs. It adopts 64-bit counters in new high-capacity groups and does not deprecate the 32-bit ones. When 64-bit counters exist, the 32-bit counters MUST still be available and report the low 32 bits.

The rules by speed: at 20,000,000 bits per second or less, 32-bit byte and packet counters MUST be used. Above that and below 650,000,000 bits per second, 32-bit packet counters and 64-bit octet counters MUST be used. At 650,000,000 bits per second or faster, both packet and octet counters MUST be 64-bit.

ifSpeed tops out at (2**31)-1 bits per second, so ifHighSpeed is added and reports speed in units of 1,000,000 bits per second. The separate multicast and broadcast counters replace the combined non-unicast counters, which are deprecated.
sections.eli5: A small odometer runs out of digits quickly on a fast car. So for fast links the counters get many more digits, and speed is reported in bigger units.

sections.title: Interface Status and Traps
sections.content:
ifOperStatus gains three states: dormant (waiting for an external event, as for on-demand interfaces), notPresent (a component, typically hardware, is missing) and lowerLayerDown (down because a lower interface in the stack is down). Together with up, down, testing and unknown that makes seven values. If ifAdminStatus is not down and ifOperStatus is down, a fault is presumed.

linkUp and linkDown traps are generated just after ifOperStatus leaves, or just before it enters, the down state, never for changes to or from notPresent. A flapping interface should be rate-limited. Because every sub-layer could send traps, ifLinkUpDownTrapEnable lets managers choose, and by default only the lowest sub-layer sends them.
sections.eli5: A plug can be on, off, napping until someone calls, missing a part, or off because the plug below it is off. An alarm rings only when the plug really goes off or comes back.

sections.title: Security and Unknown Values
sections.content:
The security section says reading the MIB is relatively innocuous, but unauthorized access to the writable objects could cause a denial of service or, combined with other breaches such as physical ones, unauthorized connectivity.

A separate rule requires honesty: when an agent does not know an object's value it MUST NOT instantiate it with an incorrect value, such as zero for an uncountable counter, and must respond with an error such as noSuchInstance. Managers MUST cope with rows that have missing columns. The ifTable cannot create interfaces itself, so media-specific MIBs that allow creation should include a RowStatus object.
sections.eli5: Looking at the list is harmless, but letting strangers change settings could switch plugs off. If the device does not know an answer, it must say so rather than make one up.

items.label: down
items.desc: Not passing packets; a fault is presumed if ifAdminStatus is not down.

items.label: unknown
items.desc: Status cannot be determined for some reason.

items.label: lowerLayerDown
items.desc: Down due to the state of lower-layer interfaces.
